title: Position: The Systemic Lack of Agency in Visual Reasoning
claim: Models passively retrieve explicit cues while agents actively find implicit evidence; a 2x2 taxonomy shows autonomous retrieval as the missing quadrant.
layout: 2 panels, left illustrative cartoon, right 2x2 quadrant matrix with highlighted missing cell
description: A hand-drawn, sketch-style figure split by a vertical line. The left panel shows a prompt box at the top, "How tall is this bottle? (Answer: 20cm)", with two arrows pointing to two identical black bottles, each standing on a table with a stack of coins beside it. On the left, the human/ideal bottle has a thought bubble that reasons from the coin (2.5cm each, 8 coins, so 20cm). A green arrow runs to the coins, and the label reads "Human/Ideal: Active Agency" in green. On the right, the VLM bottle has a thought bubble that guesses "15cm". The coins are marked with a blue hatched box, and the label reads "VLM: Passive Capacity" in red. The right panel is a 2x2 matrix. The y-axis is Cognitive Task (Perception to Reasoning) and the x-axis is Context Dependency (Explicit to Implicit). Q1 to Q3 each have a small icon. The top-right Q4, "the missing Q4: Autonomous Information Retrieval", sits in a red dashed box with a question mark. The eye goes first to the bottles and then to the red dashed Q4.
caption: Agency in visual reasoning. Left: Comparison of active agency vs. passive capacity in visual reasoning. Unlike humans actively retrieve implicit visual cues to reason about physical properties, current VLMs tend to ignore the implicit information and give wrong answers. Right: Our taxonomy highlights Autonomous Information Retrieval (Q4) as the critical gap. Success here requires visual agency, the ability to actively seek unmentioned visual evidence without explicit prompting which current models lack.
abstract: This paper argues that a systemic lack of Agency constrains the implicit reasoning capabilities of current Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Implicit reasoning refers to the ability to autonomously discover and utilize hidden visual evidence to bridge information gaps, rather than merely relying on explicitly specified targets. This capacity underlies human visual understanding and everyday reasoning. We argue that this limitation arises from a tendency to approach visual reasoning primarily as passive semantic retrieval, rather than as active, situated reasoning that depends on autonomous visual exploration. As a result, most existing benchmarks primarily assess Passive Capacity, leaving this aspect of reasoning largely unmeasured. To address this gap, we introduce the Visual Implicit Reasoning Diagnosing Benchmark (V-IRD), which targets this missing quadrant by requiring models to derive answers strictly through autonomous visual analysis. Our results show that, despite strong retrieval abilities, prominent VLMs struggle to utilize reference objects and to attend to visual evidence that requires self-directed inquiry. Simply put, strong semantic recognition does not equate to active visual exploration, revealing a critical gap in current VLMs. More information can be found at https://haoychen.github.io/Implicit-Reasoning/
